A running depth counter: each '<' increments depth, each '>' decrements it. A 'matching closing bracket' is one that occurs while depth is still positive -- order matters, since a '>' before any unmatched '<' drives depth negative. The string is correctly bracketed only if depth never goes negative and returns to exactly 0 at the end.

Per the reference, it counts how many times each distinct value appears in the list; if any value appears more than twice (count > 2), the function returns False regardless of order. Exactly two occurrences of a value is allowed; three or more is not.

Per the true spec, path A is 'less than' path B if, comparing their ordered lists of cell values position by position, A is lexicographically smaller than B. The problem guarantees the minimum path (by this lexicographic ordering) is unique, so ties by this specific ordering don't occur.

The docstring only explicitly defines tri(1)=3 as a base case; the reference handles n=0 as a separate special case, returning [1] (a list containing just the value 1) rather than computing tri(0) via the recurrence.

Per the reference, 'word' means a maximal run of characters separated by a literal space character (' '). The function checks whether the last word (after splitting on spaces) is exactly one character long and that character is an ASCII letter -- so a 'non-letter' boundary here specifically means a space character or the start/end of the string.

The reference's actual condition is n % 2 == 0 and n >= 8 -- this correctly handles negative, zero, or small positive n by simply returning False (since the smallest sum of four positive even numbers is 2+2+2+2=8), no special-casing needed.

A run of exactly 2 consecutive spaces is replaced with two underscores (one underscore per space, via the 'end - start > 0' branch); only runs of MORE than 2 consecutive spaces get collapsed to a single '-'.

Per the reference, the check for 'index is a multiple of 3' comes first and takes priority; the cube branch explicitly excludes multiples of 3 (elif i % 4 == 0 and i % 3 != 0). So an index that's a multiple of 12 (multiple of both 3 and 4) is squared, not cubed.

Per the reference's digits_sum helper, for a negative number the sign is tracked separately and applied to only the FIRST digit of the number's absolute value -- e.g. -11 has digit sum -1+1=0, not -(1+1)=-2.

A triple is any three elements a[i], a[j], a[k] of the array where the indices satisfy i < j < k (strictly increasing, three distinct positions in order); the function counts how many such index-triples have a[i]+a[j]+a[k] divisible by 3.
Per the reference, if planet1 == planet2 the function returns an empty tuple () -- the same as the case of an invalid planet name.

Per the reference, n is treated as prime if none of the integers from 2 up to n-1 evenly divide it (trial division), and n=1 is explicitly excluded via a special case (if n == 1: return y) before the loop, so 1 is never treated as prime.

Floats are excluded entirely, even whole-number floats like 3.0 -- the reference's check '.' not in str(i) filters out anything whose string representation contains a decimal point, so 3.0 (which stringifies to "3.0") is skipped regardless of its numeric value.

It refers to whole numbers that are themselves single digits (0-9) and fall within the range -- per the reference, it clamps the range to [max(2, min(a,b)), min(8, max(a,b))] and returns every even integer in that clamped range, not the individual digit characters of larger numbers.
